extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, naturalists, and students studying freshwater sponges (taxonomy, morphology, ecology)
extracted.subtask_description: Identification, natural-history description, and ecological characterization of freshwater Spongillidæ (morphology, reproductive structures, habitat, associations, and biogeography), with comparative notes on Oriental taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spicule variability in species separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Spongillidæ vary without apparent cause as regards the shape, size, and proportions of their spicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When separating species, give careful consideration to intraspecific variability of spicule morphology; spicule differences may not always indicate separate species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule structure as diagnostic character
rubrics_metrics.description: Internally the gemmule consists of a mass of cells containing food-material ... enclosed in a flask-like receptacle, the walls of which consist of two chitinous layers, a delicate inner membrane and an outer one of considerable stoutness. The mouth of the flask is closed by an extension of the inner membrane, and in some species is surrounded by a tubular extension of the external membrane known as the foraminal tubule. Externally the gemmule is usually covered by a 'pneumatic coat' ... honeycombed by spaces which contain air ... The pneumatic coat also contains the microscleres characteristic of the species; it is often limited externally by a third chitinous membrane, on which more gemmule-spicules sometimes lie parallel to the surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gemmule internal layers, pneumatic coat structure, foraminal tubule presence, microscleres and gemmule-spicule arrangement are important morphological characters for species diagnosis and comparison within Spongillidæ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule seasonality and dormancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Gemmules are produced by the freshwater sponges of Europe, N. America and Japan at the approach of winter, but in the tropical parts of India they are formed more frequently at the approach of the hot weather. After they are fully formed the sponge that has produced them dies ... In any case all of them undergo a period of quiescence before germinating. It has been found that they can be kept dry for two years without dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect geographic/climatic variation in gemmule production timing and dormancy; factor seasonality and local climate into collection schedules and experimental germination attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule-spicule mass correlated with habitat
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of the special spicules with which the gemmules of the Spongillidæ are provided appears to be not only to protect them but more especially to weight them to the extent suitable to the habits of each species. Species that inhabit running water, for example, in some cases have heavier gemmule-spicules than those that live in stagnant water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gemmule-spicule size/weight as an ecological and taxonomic indicator (heavier spicules in species adapted to running water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumatic coat morphology (granular vs cellular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except in the genus Corvospongilla and the subgenus Stratospongilla ... the pneumatic coat is either 'granular' or 'cellular.' Neither of these terms, however, must be understood in a physiological sense, for what appear to be granules in a granular coat are actually minute bubbles of air contained in little cavities in a foam-like mass of chitin (or rather spongin), while the cells in a cellular one are only larger and more regular air-spaces with thin polygonal walls and flat horizontal partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between granular and cellular pneumatic coats when describing gemmules; interpret these terms morphologically (air-space architecture) rather than physiologically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule shape, grouping and attachment as characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmules with their various coverings are usually spherical in shape, but in some species they are oval or depressed in outline. They lie as a rule free in the substance of the sponge, but in some species adhere at its base to the object to which it is attached. In some species they are joined together in groups, but in most they are quite free one from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record gemmule shape (spherical/oval/depressed), whether they are free, adherent, or grouped—these are useful diagnostic traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding morphology and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproductive buds are produced, so far as is known, by very few Spongillidæ ... In Spongilla proliferens the buds arise as thickenings of the strands of cells accompanying the radiating spicule-fibres ... the thickenings ... contain, at the earliest stage ..., all the elements of the adult organism ... except skeleton fibres, gemmules, and a dermal membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present, characterize bud origin, contents, and development (which elements are present/absent). Bud morphology can distinguish species that habitually bud (e.g., S. proliferens) from those that do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule germination triggers and experimental notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Carter found that if he cleaned gemmules with a handkerchief and placed them in water exposed to sunlight, they germinated in a few days; but in Calcutta gemmules of Spongilla alba var. bengalensis treated in this way ... did not germinate until well on in the 'rains.' Zykoff found that in Europe gemmules kept for two years were still alive and able to germinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gemmule germination can sometimes be induced by cleaning and sunlight exposure, but responses vary by species and local conditions; long dormancy (years) possible—design germination experiments accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat preferences (light/shade, current, disturbance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Favourable conditions consist in a due mixture of light and shade, a lack of disturbance such as that caused by cleaning out the pond, and above all in the presence of objects suitable for the support of sponges. ... most species prefer shade, if it be not too dense; ... Indian Spongillidæ flourish best in water shaded at the edges by trees and exposed to sunlight elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use habitat descriptors (light/shade mix, current speed, disturbance regime, availability of attachment substrates) when surveying or interpreting species distributions; note regional exceptions (e.g., some Indian species thriving in polluted or unshaded ponds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substrate attachment preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sponges are found fixed either to floating objects such as logs of wood, to vertical objects such as the stems of bulrushes and other aquatic plants, or to the tips of branches that overhang the water and become submerged during the 'rains.' ... Several Indian sponges are only found adhering to stones and rocks. ... There are at least two sponges ... which in Calcutta are only found attached to [artificial objects].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record substrate type (stones, wood, plant stems, artificial structures) when sampling; substrate preference is species-specific and influences local occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salinity tolerance as taxonomic/ecological indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Few Spongillidæ are found in salt or brackish water, but Spongilla alba var. bengalensis has been found in both, and is abundant in the latter; indeed, it has not been found in pure fresh water. Spongilla travancorica has only been found in slightly brackish water, while S. lacustris subsp. reticulata and Dosilia plumosa occur in both fresh and brackish water, although rarely in the latter. The Spongillidæ are essentially a freshwater family, and those forms that are found in any but pure fresh water must be regarded as aberrant or unusually tolerant in their habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat occurrences in brackish or saline environments as noteworthy and potentially diagnostic of tolerant/aberrant taxa; salinity tolerance informs ecological and taxonomic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of green corpuscles (Chlorella) as biological/diagnostic trait
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally believed that the green corpuscles play an important part in the nutrition of those sponges in which they occur ... these bodies have the power ... of obtaining nutritive substances direct from water and carbonic oxide through the action of sunlight. Possibly they hand on some of the nourishment thus obtained to the sponges in which they live, or benefit them by the free oxygen given out in the process, but many Spongillidæ do well without them, even when living in identical conditions with species in which they abound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record presence/absence and condition (colour intensity, response to light) of green corpuscles; treat them as potential symbionts but not universally diagnostic—presence may vary with light and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known enemies and ecological threats
rubrics_metrics.description: The neuropteroid larva (Sisyra indica) which sucks the cells of several species ... Other animals that may be enemies are a midge larva (Tanypus sp.) and certain worms that bore through the parenchyma ... If their external membrane is destroyed, they are immediately attacked by various little fish and also by snails of the genera Limnæa and Planorbis, and prawns of the genus Palæmon. Their most active and obvious enemy is a plant ... a filamentous alga that blocks up their canals by its rapid growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for predation, boring organisms, and algal overgrowth when assessing sponge health, population declines, or distributional changes; note that different enemies act under different types of injury or environmental stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interactions and handling cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponges may be of some hygienic importance in absorbing putrid organic matter ... The only harm ... is that of polluting water, of blocking up water-pipes by their growth -- a very rare occurrence, -- and of causing irritation to the human skin by means of their spicules -- a still rarer one. ... students of the freshwater sponges should be careful not to rub their eyes after handling dried specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering anthropogenic effects or practical implications, note both potential water-purifying roles and rare nuisance/health effects; advise safe handling to avoid spicule irritation and eye contact after specimen manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in identifying fossil sponges from isolated spicules
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of sponges from isolated spicules is, however, always a matter of doubt, and in some cases Ehrenberg probably assigned spicules belonging to entirely different families or even orders to the same genus, while he frequently attributed the different spicules of the same species to different genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fossil identifications based solely on isolated spicules as tentative; use multiple lines of evidence where possible and document uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (Euspongilla) microsclerifera
rubrics_metrics.description: This sponge is closely related to S. lacustris, but apparently does not produce branches. It is remarkable for the enormous number of microscleres in its parenchyma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use absence of branching and a very large number of microscleres in parenchyma as distinguishing traits for S. microsclerifera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (Euspongilla) philippinensis
rubrics_metrics.description: Related to S. alba and still more closely to S. sceptrioides ... From the former it is readily distinguished by having minutely spined megascleres, green corpuscles, slender gemmule-spicules with short spines and no free microscleres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish S. philippinensis by minutely spined megascleres, presence of green corpuscles, slender gemmule-spicules with short spines, and lack of free microscleres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (? Euspongilla) yunnanensis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparently allied to S. philippinensis but with smooth skeleton-spicules and a more delicate skeleton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate by smooth skeleton-spicules and generally more delicate skeletal construction compared with allied species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (Stratospongilla) sinensis
rubrics_metrics.description: Their gemmules are intermediate in structure between those of that subgenus and those of Euspongilla. In S. sinensis the gemmules are packed together in groups at the base of the sponge, and their spicules are smooth, stout, and gradually pointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize S. sinensis by grouped gemmules at the base and smooth, stout, gradually pointed gemmule-spicules; note intermediate gemmule structure between subgeneric types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (Stratospongilla) clementis
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmules are single and closely adherent at the base of the sponge. Their spicules are very slender and minutely spined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify S. clementis by single, closely adherent gemmules at the base and very slender, minutely spined gemmule-spicules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (? Stratospongilla) coggini
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmules apparently lack microscleres. They resemble those of S. clementis ... The skeleton-spicules are spiny and rather stout, the species being strongly developed at the two ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate S. coggini by absence of microscleres in gemmules, spiny and rather stout skeleton-spicules, and robust development at each end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Spongilla (Stratospongilla) sumatrana
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely allied to S. indica but with pointed skeleton-spicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pointed skeleton-spicules to distinguish S. sumatrana from close relatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Ephydatia fortis
rubrics_metrics.description: This species is remarkable for the great development of the spines on the shaft of the gemmule-spicules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify E. fortis by strongly developed spines along the shaft of gemmule-spicules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Ephydatia bogorensis
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmule-spicules have rather narrow flattish disks, the edge of which is feebly but closely serrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize E. bogorensis by gemmule-spicules with narrow flattish disks edged with fine serration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Ephydatia blembingia
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmules resemble those of Dosilia plumosa but are spherical. There are no free microscleres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate E. blembingia by spherical gemmules similar to Dosilia plumosa and absence of free microscleres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic characters: Tubella vesparium
rubrics_metrics.description: Closely related to T. vesparioides, but with spiny megascleres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish T. vesparium by the presence of spiny megascleres relative to close congeners.
